meta.title: Basis Points vs. Percentage Points: Convert Rates Without Mixing Units
meta.heading: Basis Points vs. Percentage Points: Convert Rates Without Mixing Units
meta.description: Understand basis points versus percentage points with rate comparisons, decimal conversions and a worked fixed-balance fee example.
meta.cardIntro: One basis point is 0.01 percentage point, so 25 bps equals 0.25% as a rate quantity and 0.0025 as a decimal. A move from 5% to 5.25% is a 25-bps absolute increase and a 5% relative increase. Use the mode that matches a conversion, a rate comparison or a proportional monetary amount.

basis-point.intro: Financial rate conversion and proportional amounts only. No live rates, compounding, mortgage payment calculation or implied time period. Relative rate change is shown only for a positive starting rate.
basis-point.answer: One basis point is 0.01 percentage point, so 25 bps equals 0.25% as a rate quantity and 0.0025 as a decimal. A move from 5% to 5.25% is a 25-bps absolute increase and a 5% relative increase. Use the mode that matches a conversion, a rate comparison or a proportional monetary amount.

sections.title: Start by identifying the unit you actually have
paragraphs: A quoted percentage, a decimal fraction and a basis-point value can represent the same rate. Enter 25 with Basis points selected, 0.25 with Percent selected, or 0.0025 with Decimal selected to describe the same quantity. Entering 0.25 as a decimal instead describes 25%, or 2,500 bps. The input-unit selection is part of the calculation, not a cosmetic label.

A percentage point describes the difference between two percentages. Basis points make small differences easier to state without ambiguous percent language. This guide concerns financial rates; the abbreviation bps can also mean bits per second in networking, which uses a different measurement entirely.

sections.title: Separate absolute rate differences from relative changes
paragraphs: Suppose a hypothetical rate rises from 5% to 5.25%. Subtract the percentages to obtain 0.25 percentage point, then multiply by 100 to obtain 25 bps. For the relative increase, divide that 0.25-point difference by the original 5% rate: 0.25 / 5 × 100 = 5%. Both numbers describe the same move, but they answer different questions.

A fall from 5% to 4.5% is a −0.5-percentage-point change, or −50 bps. Relative to a positive 5% starting rate, that is a 10% decrease. At zero, the relative division is undefined; a negative starting rate makes the everyday interpretation of percent growth problematic. The calculator retains the absolute basis-point change and omits that relative comparison.

sections.title: Apply basis points to a stated monetary base
paragraphs: For a hypothetical $200,000 base and 25 bps, calculate $200,000 × 25 / 10,000 = $500. Specify whether the context is a one-time fee, an annual charge or another stated period. The arithmetic itself does not introduce a year or a monthly billing cycle. A negative basis-point entry produces a negative proportional adjustment.

If a fee is annual and the balance stays exactly $200,000 for a full year, the simple 25-bps annual amount is $500. A changing balance, tiered fee, minimum charge or different billing convention requires more detail. A mortgage-rate difference is particularly easy to misread: $500 of simple annual rate effect is not the difference between two amortizing monthly payments.

sections.title: Use a small reconciliation before comparing offers
paragraphs: Record the original quote, its unit, the comparison quote and any stated period. Use the rate-change mode for two quoted rates, then use the amount mode only if a fixed-base proportional comparison is relevant. Keep taxes, fee scope and compounding outside a comparison unless the chosen calculator explicitly models them.

The worked cases below isolate unit conversion and rate direction. Their values are hypothetical, with no claim that any lender or fund currently offers these rates. Preset links restore the selected unit as well as the numeric input, and the CSV keeps those assumptions beside the selected result.

questions.question: How many basis points are in 1%?
questions.answer: A 1% rate quantity equals 100 basis points. A change of one percentage point also equals 100 bps; a 1% relative increase is a different comparison.

questions.question: Is 25 bps the same as 0.25%?
questions.answer: Yes as a rate quantity: 25 bps = 0.25% = 0.0025 in decimal form. A 25-bps change means 0.25 percentage point, not necessarily a 0.25% relative change.

questions.question: How do I convert a decimal to basis points?
questions.answer: Multiply the decimal fraction by 10,000. For example, 0.0025 × 10,000 = 25 bps. In Convert mode, select Decimal before entering 0.0025.

questions.question: Can basis points be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. A rate move from 5% to 4.5% is −50 bps. Conversion preserves the sign; relative change is omitted for a zero or negative starting rate.

questions.question: Does 25 bps on a mortgage equal a $500 payment change?
questions.answer: On a fixed $200,000 base, 25 bps represents $500 of proportional amount. That is not a change in monthly mortgage payment; an amortizing payment also depends on the term, balance and payment frequency.

meta.title: How to Prorate Rent: Actual Days, 30-Day Months & Leap Years
meta.heading: How to Prorate Rent: Actual Days, 30-Day Months & Leap Years
meta.description: Compare actual-month, 30-day and annual rent proration. Follow inclusive dates, leap years, cross-month calculations and rounding examples.
meta.cardIntro: Prorated rent charges only the selected billable days. With $2,000 monthly rent and January 17–31 included, the actual-calendar calculation is $2,000 / 31 × 15 = $967.74. A 30-day denominator gives $1,000 for the same dates. Use the method and billable-date convention required by your agreement and applicable rules.

prorated-rent.intro: Manual constant monthly rent and explicitly included billable dates. The selected day-count method is an assumption, not a legal ruling or a determination of lease obligations. No deposits, utilities, concessions or automatic monthly caps.
prorated-rent.answer: Prorated rent charges only the selected billable days. With $2,000 monthly rent and January 17–31 included, the actual-calendar calculation is $2,000 / 31 × 15 = $967.74. A 30-day denominator gives $1,000 for the same dates. Use the method and billable-date convention required by your agreement and applicable rules.

sections.title: Choose billable dates before choosing a formula
paragraphs: A move date alone may not tell you which days are chargeable. The calculator asks for the first and last billable days and includes both. January 17 through January 31 contains fifteen billable days. If an agreement excludes the departure day, enter the day before departure rather than silently treating the displayed end date as exclusive.

The date mode counts calendar days, not hours, so daylight-saving transitions do not create partial days. It splits an interval at month boundaries. Monthly rent stays constant across those segments; a mid-period rent increase, concession or separate utility charge requires a separate calculation. This tool does not interpret the lease or determine local legal entitlements.

sections.title: See why the denominator changes the charge
paragraphs: For $2,000 monthly rent and fifteen billable days in a 31-day month, the actual-month method uses an unrounded daily rate of $2,000 / 31 and gives $967.74 after final rounding. A fixed-30-day method divides the same monthly rent by 30 and gives $1,000. The difference comes from the denominator, not from counting different dates.

A fixed-365-year method uses twelve times monthly rent divided by 365, then multiplies by billable days. An actual-year method uses 365 or 366 according to each segment’s calendar year. These are explicit alternatives for comparison. They do not establish which convention a landlord or tenant is entitled to apply.

sections.title: Split cross-month and leap-year intervals visibly
paragraphs: For January 30 through February 2, 2026, include two January days and two February days. At $2,000 monthly rent, the actual-calendar total is $2,000 × 2/31 plus $2,000 × 2/28, or about $271.89. Applying only January’s daily rate to all four days would miss February’s denominator.

In February 2024, the actual-month denominator is 29. Fifteen days at $1,800 monthly rent give $1,800 × 15/29, or about $931.03. The actual-year method instead gives $1,800 × 12 × 15/366, or about $885.25. Both are internally consistent arithmetic conventions, so select the one that matches the agreement rather than whichever produces a preferred amount.

sections.title: Reconcile the displayed estimate with a billing record
paragraphs: The calculation retains unrounded daily rates and monthly segment charges, sums them, and rounds the displayed monetary total. For the January example, rounding $2,000 / 31 to $64.52 first and multiplying by fifteen gives $967.80, six cents more than retaining precision until the end. The segment CSV exposes the unrounded values used by this worksheet.

Known-days mode is useful when you have already confirmed the count for one calendar month. Enter the actual month length even when comparing a fixed denominator. It accepts zero billable days and returns zero charge. Use date mode for intervals spanning months or years. A fixed-30 calculation does not invent a full-month cap, and neither mode creates an invoice, security-deposit statement or legal determination.

questions.question: Do I count the move-in and move-out days?
questions.answer: This calculator includes both entered billable dates. Whether a departure day is chargeable depends on your agreement and applicable rules. If it is excluded, enter the preceding day as the last billable day.

questions.question: Should I divide rent by 30 or by the days in the month?
questions.answer: Use the method applicable to your agreement. Actual-calendar, fixed-30-day and annual methods can differ. The calculator displays the selected method and does not determine which one is legally required.

questions.question: How does a leap year affect prorated rent?
questions.answer: The actual-month method uses 29 days for February in a leap year. The actual-year method uses 366 days for that year; fixed-365 and fixed-30 methods keep their stated denominators.

questions.question: Can a 30-day calculation exceed the monthly rent?
questions.answer: Yes. Applying monthly rent / 30 to 31 actual billable days gives 31/30 of monthly rent. This worksheet imposes no cap and does not implement a 30/360 date-count convention; check any contractual cap separately.

questions.question: Why can my invoice differ by a few cents?
questions.answer: The worksheet keeps full daily-rate precision and rounds the final total for display. An invoice that rounds each daily charge or each monthly line before summing can differ; use the agreed rounding policy.

meta.title: Operating Cash Flow vs. Net Income: Working Capital & the Cash Bridge
meta.heading: Operating Cash Flow vs. Net Income: Working Capital & the Cash Bridge
meta.description: Reconcile net income to operating cash flow. Follow signed working-capital changes and cross-check the indirect and direct methods.
meta.cardIntro: Operating cash flow measures cash generated or used by the entered operating activities. In the worked reconciliation, $120,000 net income plus $30,000 adjustments minus a $20,000 operating working-capital increase gives $130,000 OCF. The same result can be reconstructed from consistent operating cash receipts and payments; it is not the same measure as profit or free cash flow.

operating-cash-flow.intro: A manual operating-cash-flow worksheet for one consistent reporting scope. Inputs require reconciled classifications; the tool does not prepare a complete accounting statement, retrieve company accounts or calculate free cash flow.
operating-cash-flow.answer: Operating cash flow measures cash generated or used by the entered operating activities. In the worked reconciliation, $120,000 net income plus $30,000 adjustments minus a $20,000 operating working-capital increase gives $130,000 OCF. The same result can be reconstructed from consistent operating cash receipts and payments; it is not the same measure as profit or free cash flow.

sections.title: Explain the gap between earnings and operating cash
paragraphs: Accrual earnings and operating cash answer different questions. A credit sale can enter revenue before collection; depreciation can reduce earnings without a current-period cash payment. A useful reconciliation identifies the specific items separating the two measures instead of assuming net income is money available in a bank account.

In our hypothetical period, net income is $120,000 and signed noncash or nonoperating adjustments total $30,000. The operating asset changes are $15,000 more receivables, $10,000 more inventory and $5,000 more other operating assets. Those increases subtract $30,000 from the cash bridge. Increases of $8,000 trade payables and $2,000 other operating liabilities add $10,000 back. The resulting OCF is $130,000.

sections.title: Enter balance changes with their actual signs
paragraphs: Every change field means ending balance minus beginning balance. An operating receivable growing from $40,000 to $55,000 is a positive $15,000 change; the worksheet subtracts it. A fall from $55,000 to $25,000 is a negative $30,000 change; the worksheet adds $30,000. Do not pre-negate an asset increase and then let the formula negate it a second time.

The same sign convention applies to liabilities, but their cash effect is opposite: an included operating payable increase adds to the indirect bridge, while a decrease subtracts. Balance-sheet differences caused by acquisitions, disposals, foreign-currency translation or other noncash changes need reconciliation first. This calculator cannot infer those adjustments from two reported balances.

sections.title: Use either component changes or an already reconciled net amount
paragraphs: For the worked case, operating assets increase $30,000 while operating liabilities increase $10,000. The increase in operating net working capital is therefore $20,000. Known Working-Capital Change mode computes $120,000 + $30,000 − $20,000, matching the component mode. Use the aggregate instead of entering its components again.

The operating definition excludes cash, cash equivalents and interest-bearing debt. Noncash adjustments are also signed: depreciation that was included in earnings can be added back, while applicable noncash income or investing gains may require subtraction. An adjustment already reflected in another line must not be counted again. The worksheet accepts your reconciled inputs; it does not select an accounting policy.

sections.title: Cross-check using receipts and payments without subtracting depreciation
paragraphs: A separately specified direct illustration uses $600,000 operating cash receipts and cash payments of $300,000 to suppliers, $100,000 to employees, $30,000 income taxes, $10,000 interest and $30,000 other operating costs. Payments total $470,000, leaving $130,000 OCF. These hypothetical amounts are deliberately consistent with the indirect example; arbitrary inputs from unrelated statements need not match.

Direct mode subtracts actual cash payments, not accrual expense totals. Do not subtract depreciation again. This U.S.-oriented illustration includes operating interest and income-tax cash payments, but classification depends on the reporting framework and transaction facts. Asset purchases, borrowing principal and owner distributions belong outside this operating worksheet. OCF therefore does not equal the entire change in cash and does not by itself establish free cash flow or distributable cash.

questions.question: What is the operating cash flow formula?
questions.answer: In this indirect worksheet, start with net income, add signed noncash and nonoperating reconciliation adjustments, then subtract the increase in operating net working capital. Direct mode subtracts operating cash payments from operating receipts.

questions.question: Does an increase in accounts receivable add or subtract cash?
questions.answer: An included operating receivables increase is subtracted in the indirect reconciliation. A decrease is entered as a negative change and adds cash, assuming the change has been reconciled for noncash and nonoperating movements.

questions.question: Do I include cash and debt in working capital?
questions.answer: Not in this worksheet’s operating net working-capital definition. Exclude cash, cash equivalents and interest-bearing debt. Include the operating asset and operating liability items required by your reconciliation.

questions.question: Can operating cash flow be negative when net income is positive?
questions.answer: Yes. A large operating working-capital increase or other cash-consuming adjustment can outweigh positive net income. A negative result alone does not identify its cause or prove insolvency.

questions.question: Is operating cash flow the same as free cash flow?
questions.answer: No. Capital expenditure is a separate investing cash-flow item. Free cash flow commonly adjusts operating cash flow for capital spending, but definitions vary and this calculator does not label OCF as free cash flow.
